questions.question: You are initializing a new Kubernetes control plane with kubeadm. You want the API server to advertise the IP address 10.0.1.100 to worker nodes. Which kubeadm init flag should you use?
options: --apiserver-bind-address=10.0.1.100
--apiserver-advertise-address=10.0.1.100
--control-plane-endpoint=10.0.1.100
questions.explanation: --apiserver-advertise-address tells kubeadm which IP address the API server should advertise to members of the cluster. --apiserver-bind-address controls which interface it binds to. --control-plane-endpoint is used for HA setups with a load balancer DNS/VIP. --node-ip is a kubelet flag, not a kubeadm init flag.

questions.question: A worker node needs to join an existing cluster but the bootstrap token has expired. Which kubeadm command generates a new join token?
options: kubeadm token generate
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
kubeadm init --regenerate-token
kubeadm join --create-token
questions.explanation: 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' creates a new bootstrap token and prints the complete 'kubeadm join' command including the token and CA cert hash. 'kubeadm token generate' only outputs a random token string — it does not register it with the cluster. The other options do not exist.

questions.question: You need to take a snapshot backup of etcd running as a static pod. The etcd data directory is /var/lib/etcd and certificates are in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. Which command correctly creates the snapshot?
options: etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
etcdctl backup --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd --backup-dir=/backup/etcd.db
kubectl exec -n kube-system etcd-master -- etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db
etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd
questions.explanation: etcdctl snapshot save requires the endpoint and TLS credentials (--cacert, --cert, --key) to connect to the running etcd cluster. Without TLS flags, etcdctl will be rejected. 'etcdctl backup' is an old v2 API syntax no longer used. Running via kubectl exec without passing the certs would also fail. --data-dir is not a valid flag for snapshot save.

questions.question: After restoring an etcd snapshot to a new data directory /var/lib/etcd-restore, what must you update so that the etcd static pod uses the restored data?
options: Run 'systemctl restart etcd' on the control plane node
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml and update the --data-dir flag and the hostPath volume to point to /var/lib/etcd-restore
Delete the etcd pod and let the controller manager recreate it with the new data
Run 'kubeadm etcd restore /var/lib/etcd-restore' to reload the configuration
questions.explanation: etcd runs as a static pod managed by the kubelet. Its manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml defines both the --data-dir argument and the hostPath mount. You must update both the --data-dir flag value and the hostPath volume source to point to the restored directory. The kubelet detects the manifest change and restarts the pod automatically.

questions.question: You are upgrading a cluster from Kubernetes 1.29 to 1.30. Which is the correct order of operations?
options: Upgrade all worker nodes first, then upgrade the control plane
Upgrade kubeadm on the control plane, run 'kubeadm upgrade apply', then upgrade kubelet and kubectl on control plane, then upgrade workers
Upgrade kubelet on all nodes first, then upgrade kubeadm last
Run 'kubectl upgrade cluster --version=1.30' from any node with cluster-admin access
questions.explanation: The correct upgrade order is: (1) upgrade kubeadm on the control plane node, (2) run 'kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.x' which upgrades cluster components, (3) upgrade kubelet and kubectl on the control plane, (4) then repeat kubelet/kubectl upgrades on each worker node. Workers must never be upgraded before the control plane, as older control planes cannot manage newer kubelets.

questions.question: You need to grant a ServiceAccount named 'deploy-bot' in the 'ci' namespace read-only access to Deployments across all namespaces. What combination of resources should you create?
options: A Role and RoleBinding in the 'ci' namespace
A ClusterRole with get/list/watch on deployments, and a RoleBinding in the 'ci' namespace
A ClusterRole with get/list/watch on deployments, and a ClusterRoleBinding referencing the ServiceAccount
A Role with get/list/watch on deployments in every namespace, and a ClusterRoleBinding
questions.explanation: To grant cluster-wide access, you need a ClusterRole (defines permissions at cluster scope) and a ClusterRoleBinding (binds the subject across all namespaces). A RoleBinding—even referencing a ClusterRole—only grants access within the binding's namespace. Roles themselves are namespace-scoped and cannot grant cluster-wide access.

questions.question: A developer reports that 'kubectl get pods' returns 'Error from server (Forbidden)'. Their kubeconfig context is correct and points to the cluster. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The kubelet on their local machine is not running
The developer's user or ServiceAccount lacks a Role or ClusterRole binding granting 'get' on pods
The kube-apiserver certificate has expired
The developer needs to run 'kubectl auth login' to refresh credentials
questions.explanation: A 403 Forbidden error means the request reached the API server but was denied by the RBAC authorizer. This indicates the subject (user/ServiceAccount) has no Role or ClusterRole binding that grants the 'get' verb on the 'pods' resource. A certificate expiry would produce a TLS error, not Forbidden. 'kubectl auth login' is not a standard Kubernetes command.

questions.question: You need to verify what actions a ServiceAccount 'reporter' in namespace 'monitoring' can perform. Which kubectl command checks if it can list pods in that namespace?
options: kubectl get rolebindings -n monitoring | grep reporter
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:reporter -n monitoring
kubectl describe serviceaccount reporter -n monitoring
kubectl auth check --user=reporter --verb=list --resource=pods -n monitoring
questions.explanation: 'kubectl auth can-i' with --as impersonates the given subject and returns yes/no. The ServiceAccount must be specified in the format system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. 'kubectl get rolebindings' would require manual parsing and wouldn't show effective permissions from ClusterRoleBindings. 'kubectl describe serviceaccount' only shows metadata.

questions.question: The kube-apiserver certificate is about to expire. You are using kubeadm. Which command renews all control plane certificates?
options: kubeadm certs renew all
openssl x509 -signkey /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -out /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt
kubectl certificate approve all
kubeadm init phase certs all --cert-renew
questions.explanation: 'kubeadm certs renew all' renews all kubeadm-managed certificates and is the official supported method. After renewal, static pod manifests must be refreshed (usually by restarting kubelet or moving/restoring the manifest files) so the components pick up the new certs. The openssl command would not properly update all cert fields. 'kubectl certificate approve' is for approving CSRs, not renewal.

questions.question: You have multiple clusters defined in your kubeconfig. You need to temporarily switch to a cluster named 'prod-cluster' for the next few commands. Which command sets the active context without permanently modifying the config?
options: kubectl config use-context prod-cluster
export KUBECONFIG=/etc/kubernetes/prod.config
kubectl --context=prod-cluster get pods
kubectl config set-context --current --cluster=prod-cluster
questions.explanation: Using --context=prod-cluster as a per-command flag is the best approach for temporary context switching without modifying any configuration. 'kubectl config use-context' permanently changes the active context in the kubeconfig file. Exporting KUBECONFIG changes the environment for the entire shell session, not just one command. 'kubectl config set-context --current' modifies the current context's fields.

questions.question: When bootstrapping a cluster with kubeadm, which flag allows you to specify a custom pod network CIDR for the CNI plugin?
options: --service-cidr
--pod-network-cidr
--cluster-cidr
--network-plugin-cidr
questions.explanation: --pod-network-cidr defines the IP range for pod networking. This value is passed to the CNI plugin (e.g., Calico, Flannel). --service-cidr defines the range for Service ClusterIPs. --cluster-cidr is an internal kube-controller-manager flag, not a kubeadm init flag. --network-plugin-cidr does not exist.

questions.question: You need to prevent new pods from being scheduled on a node 'worker-3' while allowing existing pods to continue running, so you can perform maintenance. Which command achieves this?
options: kubectl taint nodes worker-3 maintenance=true:NoExecute
kubectl cordon worker-3
kubectl drain worker-3
kubectl label nodes worker-3 schedulable=false
questions.explanation: 'kubectl cordon' marks the node as Unschedulable, preventing new pods from being assigned to it, while leaving existing pods running. 'kubectl drain' both cordons the node AND evicts existing pods (too disruptive if you want to keep running pods). A NoExecute taint would evict pods that lack the toleration. Labels do not affect scheduling by themselves.

questions.question: A static pod manifest placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ is not starting. The pod does not appear in 'kubectl get pods -A'. What should you check first?
options: Verify the pod has a valid ServiceAccount token mounted
Check the kubelet logs on the node where the manifest was placed, using 'journalctl -u kubelet'
Check the kube-scheduler logs for scheduling errors
Confirm the pod is listed in 'kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending'
questions.explanation: Static pods are managed entirely by the kubelet, not by the API server scheduler. If a static pod isn't starting, the kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) will show parsing errors, file permission issues, or image pull problems. The kube-scheduler is not involved in static pod lifecycle. Static pods may briefly not appear in kubectl if the kubelet hasn't registered the mirror pod yet.

questions.question: You want to add a second control plane node to an existing cluster for high availability. After running 'kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs' on the primary control plane, what join command format should you use on the new control plane node?
options: kubeadm join <endpoint>:<port> --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
kubeadm join <endpoint>:<port> --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> --control-plane --certificate-key <cert-key>
kubeadm join --control-plane --copy-certs-from=<primary-node-ip>
kubeadm init --join --control-plane-endpoint=<endpoint>
questions.explanation: Joining a control plane node requires --control-plane (to promote the node) and --certificate-key (to decrypt the uploaded certificates from the cluster). Without --certificate-key, kubeadm won't copy the PKI certificates to the new control plane node. The plain join command (option A) is for worker nodes only.

questions.question: You need to view the current kubeadm cluster configuration stored in the cluster. In which ConfigMap and namespace is this stored?
options: ConfigMap 'cluster-info' in namespace 'default'
ConfigMap 'kubeadm-config' in namespace 'kube-system'
ConfigMap 'kube-config' in namespace 'kube-public'
ConfigMap 'cluster-config' in namespace 'kube-node-lease'
questions.explanation: kubeadm stores the cluster configuration in a ConfigMap named 'kubeadm-config' in the 'kube-system' namespace. You can inspect it with 'kubectl get configmap kubeadm-config -n kube-system -o yaml'. The 'cluster-info' ConfigMap in 'kube-public' contains the discovery endpoint but not the full kubeadm configuration.

questions.question: A Deployment named 'web-app' has 5 replicas but only 3 pods are running. 'kubectl describe deployment web-app' shows the ReplicaSet has 5 desired but 3 available. What is the most likely next diagnostic step?
options: Run 'kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-app' immediately
Check 'kubectl get pods' for the deployment's pods and look for non-Running states, then 'kubectl describe pod <pod-name>' for events
Scale the deployment down to 3 replicas to match the current state
Delete and recreate the Deployment with the same spec
questions.explanation: When a Deployment's desired replica count exceeds available, the pods themselves hold the diagnostic information. 'kubectl get pods' filtered to the deployment's selector reveals pod states (Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, etc.), and 'kubectl describe pod' shows events with specific error messages like image pull failures, resource constraints, or node affinity issues.

questions.question: You need a DaemonSet to run on every node including control plane nodes, which have the taint 'node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule'. What must you add to the DaemonSet pod spec?
options: Set nodeSelector to include control-plane nodes explicitly
Add a toleration for 'node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' with effect 'NoSchedule'
Set hostNetwork: true in the pod spec
Add the annotation 'scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/tolerations' to the DaemonSet metadata
questions.explanation: Taints prevent pods from being scheduled unless the pod spec includes a matching toleration. To run on tainted control plane nodes, the DaemonSet's pod template must include a toleration with key 'node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane' and effect 'NoSchedule'. nodeSelector selects by label, not taint, and wouldn't overcome the taint restriction.

questions.question: A Job must run exactly 6 pod completions with no more than 2 pods running at the same time. Which Job spec fields should you configure?
options: spec.completions: 6 and spec.parallelism: 2
spec.replicas: 6 and spec.maxSurge: 2
spec.backoffLimit: 6 and spec.concurrencyPolicy: 2
spec.completions: 6 and spec.activeDeadlineSeconds: 2
questions.explanation: 'completions' sets how many successful pod completions are required for the Job to be considered finished. 'parallelism' caps the number of pods that can run simultaneously. Together, completions: 6 and parallelism: 2 will run 2 pods at a time until 6 succeed. 'replicas' and 'maxSurge' are Deployment fields. 'concurrencyPolicy' is a CronJob field.

questions.question: A pod is stuck in 'Pending' state. 'kubectl describe pod my-pod' shows: 'Warning FailedScheduling: 0/4 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient memory.' The pod requests 8Gi memory. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Add a toleration to the pod spec to bypass resource checks
Either add a node with sufficient memory to the cluster, or reduce the pod's memory request if the workload allows it
Set spec.priorityClassName to system-cluster-critical to force scheduling
Increase the pod's memory limit while keeping the request the same
questions.explanation: The scheduler checks that a node has enough allocatable memory to satisfy the pod's request. If no node has 8Gi free, the pod stays Pending indefinitely. The correct fixes are: add a larger node, or reduce the memory request if the application genuinely needs less. Tolerations bypass taints, not resource constraints. PriorityClass can preempt lower-priority pods but won't create memory that doesn't exist. Increasing only the limit doesn't change the request.

questions.question: You want a pod to prefer scheduling on nodes labeled 'disktype=ssd' but still schedule on other nodes if no SSD nodes are available. Which scheduling construct should you use?
options: nodeSelector: disktype: ssd
A required NodeAffinity with matchExpressions on disktype=ssd
A preferred NodeAffinity (preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) with matchExpressions on disktype=ssd
A taint 'disktype=ssd:NoSchedule' on SSD nodes with a matching toleration on the pod
questions.explanation: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is a 'soft' affinity rule. The scheduler tries to place the pod on a matching node but falls back to other nodes if needed. nodeSelector and requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution are hard constraints — the pod won't schedule if no matching node exists. Taints repel pods, not attract them.

questions.question: A StatefulSet 'db' has 3 replicas. You notice that 'db-2' is stuck in Pending while 'db-0' and 'db-1' are Running. What is the default StatefulSet behavior that causes this sequencing?
options: StatefulSets require all PVCs to be bound before any pod starts
By default, StatefulSets use OrderedReady pod management: each pod must be Running and Ready before the next is created
StatefulSet pods must run on different nodes, and node-2 has insufficient resources
The StatefulSet waits for a rolling update to complete before creating new pods
questions.explanation: The default podManagementPolicy for StatefulSets is 'OrderedReady'. Pods are created sequentially (0, 1, 2...) and each must be Running and Ready before the next pod is started. If db-1 becomes Ready but db-2 is Pending, db-2 itself has an issue (likely a PVC binding failure or scheduling issue) — it's not being held back by db-1.

questions.question: A CronJob is configured with 'schedule: "*/5 * * * *"' but jobs are piling up because each run takes longer than 5 minutes. Which field prevents concurrent job executions?
options: spec.jobTemplate.spec.backoffLimit: 0
spec.concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
spec.successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 1
spec.startingDeadlineSeconds: 300
questions.explanation: 'concurrencyPolicy: Forbid' prevents a new job from being created if the previous one hasn't finished yet. The default is 'Allow' which runs overlapping jobs. 'Replace' would cancel the running job and start a new one. 'backoffLimit' controls retry behavior on failures. 'successfulJobsHistoryLimit' controls how many completed jobs to keep. 'startingDeadlineSeconds' is a deadline for starting a missed job.

questions.question: You want to prevent a specific pod from being co-located on the same node as any pod labeled 'app=database'. Which pod spec field achieves this?
options: nodeAffinity with a requiredDuringScheduling rule matching app=database
podAntiAffinity with a requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution rule matching app=database
A taint on database pods with effect NoSchedule
topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 0
questions.explanation: podAntiAffinity with requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution instructs the scheduler to never place this pod on a node where a pod matching the label selector is already running. nodeAffinity targets node labels, not pod labels. Taints on one pod don't affect another pod's scheduling. topologySpreadConstraints balance spread but don't enforce strict anti-colocation with label-matched pods.

questions.question: A pod spec defines: resources: requests: cpu: '100m' limits: cpu: '200m'. The pod is running on a node under heavy CPU pressure. What happens to the pod's CPU usage?
options: The pod is OOMKilled because it exceeded its memory allocation
The pod is evicted from the node to free up CPU for higher-priority workloads
The pod's CPU usage is throttled at 200m — it cannot use more, but it is not killed
The container runtime kills the container and reports a CrashLoopBackOff
questions.explanation: CPU is a compressible resource. When a container exceeds its CPU limit, the Linux kernel throttles it (using CFS bandwidth control) — it slows down but is not killed. This is different from memory: if a container exceeds its memory limit, it is OOMKilled. CPU throttling can cause latency issues but the pod continues to run.

questions.question: You need a ClusterIP Service for an application but want to define your own cluster IP address (e.g., 10.96.100.50). Which Service spec field allows this?
options: spec.externalIPs: ['10.96.100.50']
spec.clusterIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.loadBalancerIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.internalIP: '10.96.100.50'
questions.explanation: spec.clusterIP allows you to set a specific IP address for a ClusterIP Service, provided the address is within the configured service CIDR and is not already in use. spec.externalIPs exposes the service on additional IPs outside the cluster. spec.loadBalancerIP is for cloud LoadBalancer Services. spec.internalIP is not a valid Service field.

questions.question: A NodePort Service is created for a web application. A developer cannot reach the application at <NodeIP>:30080 from outside the cluster. The pod is Running and the Service endpoint is listed. What should you check next?
options: The pod's readinessProbe configuration
Whether the firewall or security group on the node allows inbound traffic on port 30080
The Service's clusterIP assignment
Whether kube-proxy is configured for IPVS instead of iptables mode
questions.explanation: If the pod is Running and the Service endpoint exists (meaning kube-proxy has created the iptables/IPVS rules), the most common remaining cause of NodePort inaccessibility from outside is a firewall or cloud security group blocking the port. On cloud providers, inbound rules for the NodePort range (default 30000-32767) must be explicitly allowed.

questions.question: You create an Ingress resource but HTTP requests to the defined host are returning 404. The Ingress controller pod is running. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Ingress resource needs a LoadBalancer Service instead of ClusterIP
The Ingress resource does not specify an ingressClassName matching the deployed controller, or the backend Service name/port is incorrect
Ingress resources require TLS to be configured before they become active
The kube-proxy must be restarted to pick up the new Ingress rules
questions.explanation: Common Ingress 404 causes are: (1) missing or wrong ingressClassName so the controller ignores the resource, (2) the backend service name or port number in the Ingress spec doesn't match the actual Service, or (3) the path rules don't match incoming requests. kube-proxy does not process Ingress rules — that's the Ingress controller's job. TLS is optional.

questions.question: A NetworkPolicy is applied to pods labeled 'app=api'. After applying the policy, the API pods can no longer reach the database pods labeled 'app=db' on port 5432. The policy spec has an empty 'egress: []' array. Why?
options: NetworkPolicies only apply to ingress traffic by default
An empty 'egress: []' array combined with 'policyTypes: [Egress]' blocks all egress traffic including to the database
The policy must be in the same namespace as the database pods to allow traffic
NetworkPolicies do not apply to TCP traffic on port 5432 without explicit protocol specification
questions.explanation: In Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, if 'policyTypes' includes 'Egress' and the 'egress' array is empty, all egress traffic from the selected pods is denied. An empty array means 'no rules match', which results in a default deny. To allow egress to the database, you must add an egress rule specifying the db pod selector and port 5432.

questions.question: Pods in namespace 'frontend' cannot resolve the DNS name 'backend-svc.backend.svc.cluster.local'. Pods in other namespaces resolve it fine. What should you check first?
options: Whether a NetworkPolicy in the 'frontend' namespace is blocking egress to port 53
Whether the CoreDNS ConfigMap has a broken stub zone configuration
Whether the 'backend' Service has a clusterIP assigned
Whether the 'frontend' namespace has a ResourceQuota limiting pod creation
questions.explanation: If only pods in a specific namespace cannot perform DNS resolution, a NetworkPolicy blocking egress to UDP/TCP port 53 (DNS) is the most likely culprit. CoreDNS issues would affect all namespaces. The Service having a clusterIP is necessary for DNS, but since other namespaces resolve it fine, the Service is functional. ResourceQuota limits workloads, not DNS.

questions.question: You need to expose a Service externally using a cloud provider's load balancer. Which Service type should you use?
options: NodePort
ClusterIP with an ExternalName
LoadBalancer
ExternalName
questions.explanation: Service type LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer (on supported providers like AWS, GCP, Azure) and assigns it an external IP. NodePort exposes the service on each node's IP at a static port but requires you to manage your own external load balancer. ExternalName creates a CNAME alias to an external DNS name. ClusterIP is internal-only.

questions.question: CoreDNS is running but pods cannot resolve external hostnames like 'google.com'. Internal service names resolve fine. What is the most likely cause?
options: The CoreDNS Corefile is missing the 'kubernetes' plugin
CoreDNS cannot forward queries to upstream DNS servers — check the 'forward' directive in the Corefile and ensure the upstream resolvers are reachable from the CoreDNS pods
The ndots setting in the pod's /etc/resolv.conf is set too high
External DNS resolution requires a NodePort service for CoreDNS
questions.explanation: CoreDNS handles internal Kubernetes DNS via the 'kubernetes' plugin and forwards external queries to upstream resolvers via the 'forward' plugin. If internal names resolve but external ones don't, the forward plugin is likely misconfigured or the upstream DNS servers (typically 8.8.8.8 or the node's DNS) are unreachable from the CoreDNS pods — often a NetworkPolicy issue or wrong upstream address.

questions.question: You need a Service that maps requests for 'legacy.internal' to an external hostname 'legacy.example.com' without proxying traffic. Which Service type achieves this?
options: LoadBalancer with an annotation pointing to legacy.example.com
ExternalName with spec.externalName: legacy.example.com
ClusterIP with an endpoints object pointing to the external IP
Headless Service with a manual DNS CNAME record
questions.explanation: An ExternalName Service creates a CNAME DNS entry in CoreDNS. When pods query the service name, they receive a CNAME pointing to spec.externalName. No proxying or IP allocation occurs. This is useful for abstracting external services. A manual Endpoints object would require knowing the external IP, not DNS name. Headless services return pod IPs, not CNAMEs.

questions.question: You deploy a CNI plugin and observe that pods on different nodes cannot communicate. Pods on the same node communicate fine. What is the most likely issue?
options: The kube-proxy daemonset is not running on all nodes
The CNI plugin has not propagated routing rules or overlay network configuration between nodes — check CNI pod logs and node routing tables
The kubelet on worker nodes is not running
The kube-apiserver is missing the --allow-privileged=true flag
questions.explanation: Intra-node pod communication working but cross-node failing is a classic CNI routing issue. The CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, Weave, etc.) is responsible for establishing routes between nodes so pods on different nodes can reach each other. Issues include BGP peering failures (Calico), VXLAN setup failures (Flannel), or missing routes in the OS routing table. kube-proxy handles Service routing, not pod-to-pod communication.

questions.question: A PersistentVolumeClaim is stuck in 'Pending' state. 'kubectl describe pvc my-pvc' shows: 'no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set'. What is missing?
options: The PVC needs a nodeAffinity selector to find a node with local storage
The PVC must specify either a storageClassName matching an existing StorageClass, or a pre-existing PV that satisfies the claim's access mode and capacity
The PVC needs an annotation 'volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-provisioner'
A ReadWriteMany access mode must be set for the claim to be bound
questions.explanation: A PVC binds either to a dynamically provisioned volume (requires a storageClassName referencing a StorageClass with a provisioner) or to a static PV that matches the claim's access mode, capacity, and any label selectors. With no storageClassName and no matching PV, the PVC cannot be bound. Setting storageClassName: '' explicitly opts out of dynamic provisioning.

questions.question: A PersistentVolume is created with accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] and capacity: 10Gi. A PVC requests 5Gi with accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]. Will the PVC bind to this PV?
options: No, the PVC capacity must exactly match the PV capacity
Yes, the PVC will bind because the PV satisfies the access mode and the PV capacity (10Gi) is greater than or equal to the requested 5Gi
No, ReadWriteOnce only allows binding when capacities are equal
Yes, but the PV will be resized down to 5Gi to match the PVC
questions.explanation: Kubernetes binds a PVC to a PV if the PV's access modes are a superset of the claim's, and the PV capacity is greater than or equal to the requested amount. The PV is not resized — the PVC gets access to the full 10Gi volume even though it only requested 5Gi. This is why over-provisioning is possible with static PVs.

questions.question: You need a volume that is shared between two containers in the same pod and is deleted when the pod is removed. Which volume type should you use?
options: hostPath
persistentVolumeClaim
emptyDir
configMap
questions.explanation: emptyDir is an ephemeral volume created when a pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the pod is removed. It is shared between all containers in the pod, making it ideal for inter-container communication or scratch space. hostPath persists on the node after pod deletion. PVCs persist independently. configMap mounts read-only configuration data.

questions.question: A StorageClass has 'reclaimPolicy: Retain'. After a PVC is deleted, what happens to the bound PV?
options: The PV is automatically deleted along with its underlying storage
The PV transitions to 'Released' status and the data is preserved, but the PV cannot be rebound to a new PVC until it is manually cleaned up
The PV is immediately available for binding to a new PVC
The PV status remains 'Bound' until an administrator manually deletes it
questions.explanation: With reclaimPolicy: Retain, when a PVC is deleted the PV transitions to 'Released' status. The actual storage data is preserved. However, the PV cannot be rebound automatically because it still contains a claimRef from the old PVC. An administrator must manually delete the PV (and optionally clean the data) before it can be reused. With 'Delete', the PV and underlying storage are removed automatically.

questions.question: You need to mount a secret as a volume in a pod so the application can read the secret values as files. Which volume type and mount configuration achieves this?
options: Use an emptyDir volume and copy secret data into it with an init container
Use a 'secret' volume type referencing the Secret name, and mount it at the desired path in the container
Use a configMap volume referencing the Secret name
Secrets can only be injected as environment variables, not as files
questions.explanation: Kubernetes supports a 'secret' volume type that mounts secret keys as files in the specified directory. Each key in the Secret becomes a file whose contents are the secret value. This is useful for certificates, private keys, or any file-based credential. Secrets can also be injected as environment variables, but the question asks specifically for file mounting.

questions.question: A pod's container is in 'CrashLoopBackOff' state. 'kubectl logs my-pod' shows the application exiting with 'Permission denied: /data/config.yaml'. The volume is a hostPath mount. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add securityContext.runAsRoot: true to the container spec
Set the hostPath volume type to 'DirectoryOrCreate' instead of 'Directory'
Add a securityContext to the pod or container specifying the correct fsGroup or runAsUser that has permission to read the file on the host
Change the volume type from hostPath to emptyDir
questions.explanation: A permission denied error on a volume mount usually means the process running in the container doesn't have the OS-level permissions to read the file. Setting pod securityContext.fsGroup changes the group ownership of mounted volumes, or runAsUser can match the file's owner UID. Running as root is a security risk and may not match the file permissions. 'DirectoryOrCreate' only affects whether the directory is created if missing.

questions.question: A pod is in 'OOMKilled' status. 'kubectl describe pod crashed-pod' shows 'Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled'. What does this indicate and what is the correct remediation?
options: The pod exceeded its CPU limit; increase the CPU limit in the pod spec
The container exceeded its memory limit; increase the memory limit or reduce the application's memory usage
The node ran out of disk space; clear /var/lib/docker on the node
The pod's liveness probe failed; adjust the probe timeouts
questions.explanation: OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's Out-Of-Memory killer terminated the container because it exceeded the memory limit set in the pod spec. The kernel sends SIGKILL (exit code 137) to the process. The fix is to either increase the memory limit to allow the application more headroom, or profile and reduce the application's memory usage. CPU exhaustion results in throttling, not killing.

questions.question: A node shows status 'NotReady'. You SSH into the node and run 'systemctl status kubelet'. It shows 'Active: failed'. What is your next diagnostic step?
options: Run 'kubectl describe node <node-name>' from the control plane
Run 'journalctl -u kubelet -n 100' to view the kubelet's recent log output for error messages
Delete and recreate the node object in Kubernetes
Restart the container runtime (containerd/docker) on the node
questions.explanation: Since you're already on the node and kubelet has failed, 'journalctl -u kubelet -n 100' is the correct next step to read the kubelet's logs and understand why it crashed. Common causes include misconfigured kubelet flags, certificate issues, or connectivity to the API server. Restarting containerd might be needed later but without reading logs first, it's a guess. 'kubectl describe node' won't help if kubelet isn't reporting.

questions.question: After a kubelet restart, a previously Running pod is now in 'Unknown' state for 5 minutes. What most likely caused this state?
options: The pod's containers have all exited with code 0
The node's kubelet stopped reporting to the API server; the node controller marks pods Unknown after the NodeMonitorGracePeriod expires
The pod's liveness probe has failed 3 times
The pod was manually set to Unknown by an administrator
questions.explanation: The 'Unknown' pod phase indicates the control plane cannot determine the pod's state because the node's kubelet has stopped sending heartbeats. After the NodeMonitorGracePeriod (default 40s), the node is marked NotReady. After further timeout (pod-eviction-timeout, default 5 minutes), pods are marked Unknown. Liveness probe failures cause pod restarts, not Unknown state. Administrators cannot manually set pod phase.

questions.question: A pod in 'ImagePullBackOff' state is failing to pull image 'registry.company.com/app:v1.2'. The image exists and credentials are correct. What should you check?
options: Whether the pod has a valid ServiceAccount
Whether an imagePullSecret referencing a docker-registry Secret with credentials for 'registry.company.com' is specified in the pod spec or ServiceAccount
Whether the image tag 'v1.2' uses semantic versioning
Whether the pod's nodeSelector matches a node with internet access
questions.explanation: ImagePullBackOff for a private registry almost always means missing or incorrect imagePullSecrets. You must create a Secret of type 'kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson' with credentials for the registry, then reference it in the pod spec under 'imagePullSecrets' or attach it to the ServiceAccount. The exponential backoff in 'ImagePullBackOff' (vs 'ErrImagePull') indicates repeated failed attempts.

questions.question: You run 'kubectl get events -n production --sort-by=.lastTimestamp' and see repeated 'FailedMount: Unable to attach or mount volumes'. The pod uses a PVC backed by an NFS PV. What is the most likely cause?
options: The PVC's access mode is ReadWriteOnce but multiple pods are trying to mount it
The NFS server is unreachable from the nodes, or the NFS export path/options are misconfigured
The pod's init container is preventing the main container from starting
The StorageClass has a bindingMode of WaitForFirstConsumer
questions.explanation: FailedMount errors for NFS volumes typically indicate the kubelet cannot connect to the NFS server (network issue, firewall, NFS server down) or the export path/mount options in the PV spec are wrong. Access mode issues would appear at PVC binding time, not mount time. WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding but doesn't cause mount failures after binding.

questions.question: A deployment rolling update is stuck. 'kubectl rollout status deployment/api' hangs showing '1 old replicas are pending termination'. What kubectl command would help you investigate which pod is blocking the rollout?
options: kubectl get replicasets -l app=api
kubectl describe deployment api and then kubectl describe pod <old-pod-name> to look at termination events
kubectl rollout pause deployment/api
kubectl delete replicaset <old-rs-name>
questions.explanation: A stuck rolling update with old replicas pending termination usually means a pod is not terminating cleanly — it could be ignoring SIGTERM, a preStop hook is hanging, or terminationGracePeriodSeconds is very large. Describing the old pod reveals events like 'Stopping container' and any hook execution issues. 'kubectl get replicasets' shows replica counts but not the blocking reason.

questions.question: You need to run a temporary debug container in a running pod 'web-pod' to troubleshoot a networking issue without restarting the pod. Which command should you use?
options: kubectl exec -it web-pod -- /bin/sh
kubectl debug -it web-pod --image=busybox --target=web-container
kubectl attach web-pod -c debug
kubectl run debug --image=busybox --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeName":"<node>"}}'  --rm -it
questions.explanation: 'kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=<image>' injects an ephemeral container into a running pod without restarting it. This is ideal when the main container lacks debugging tools. The --target flag shares the process namespace with the target container. 'kubectl exec' requires the tools to already be in the container image. An ephemeral container shares the pod's network namespace, making it perfect for network debugging.

questions.question: The kube-scheduler pod is not running after a cluster upgrade. It is defined as a static pod. Where would you find its manifest to investigate?
options: /etc/systemd/system/kube-scheduler.service
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
/var/lib/kubelet/config/kube-scheduler.yaml
/opt/kubernetes/scheduler/kube-scheduler.yaml
questions.explanation: In a kubeadm-provisioned cluster, all control plane components (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, etcd) run as static pods. Their manifests are in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ on the control plane node. The kubelet watches this directory and manages the pods. A misconfiguration in the YAML (e.g., wrong image tag, invalid flag) would prevent the scheduler from starting.

questions.question: A pod has the following in its spec: 'livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /healthz port: 8080 initialDelaySeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 3'. The pod enters CrashLoopBackOff shortly after start. Logs show the app starts fine. What is the most likely issue?
options: The /healthz endpoint is returning HTTP 500 before the app fully initializes, and the probe is restarting the container
The liveness probe port 8080 is blocked by a NetworkPolicy
The failureThreshold of 3 is too low and must be at least 5 for any probe
The container is exceeding its memory limit during startup
questions.explanation: If the application logs show it starts fine but the pod keeps restarting, a failing liveness probe is the most likely culprit. If /healthz returns a non-2xx status (e.g., 500) during initialization — even after 5 seconds — the probe will fail and after 3 failures Kubernetes restarts the container. The fix is to increase initialDelaySeconds or use a startupProbe to give the app time to be ready.

questions.question: You need to check why the kube-controller-manager is continuously restarting. Which command retrieves its previous container's logs?
options: kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-master
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-master --previous
journalctl -u kube-controller-manager -b -1
kubectl describe pod -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-master
questions.explanation: 'kubectl logs --previous' (or -p) retrieves the logs from the previously terminated container instance. This is essential for CrashLoopBackOff diagnostics — the current container may not have any useful logs yet. 'kubectl describe pod' shows events but not the full log output. journalctl is for systemd services; as a static pod, the controller-manager logs are accessed via kubectl.

questions.question: A node's disk pressure condition is True. You run 'kubectl describe node worker-1' and see 'DiskPressure: True'. As a result, some pods are being evicted. What is the underlying cause and immediate remediation?
options: The node's CPU usage is too high; scale down workloads on the node
The node's filesystem (typically /var/lib/kubelet or /var/lib/docker or container image storage) is near capacity; free up disk space by removing unused images, logs, or data
The node's memory is exhausted; add swap space to the node
The kubelet's --disk-pressure-threshold is set too low; increase it in the kubelet config
questions.explanation: DiskPressure is triggered when the kubelet detects available disk space on the node falls below the eviction threshold (default: imagefs.available < 15%). Common culprits are accumulated container images, large log files, or application data. Remediation includes: 'crictl rmi --prune' to remove unused images, cleaning old logs, or expanding the disk. The kubelet evicts pods to free up space.

questions.question: You observe that a pod is being evicted every few hours. 'kubectl describe pod' shows 'Reason: Evicted' and the message references memory pressure. The pod has no resource requests set. What is the recommended fix?
options: Set the pod's restart policy to Never to prevent eviction
Set explicit memory requests and limits on the pod, and use a PodDisruptionBudget to protect it from eviction
Move the pod to the kube-system namespace so it gets higher priority
Set imagePullPolicy to Never to reduce memory overhead during image pulls
questions.explanation: Pods without resource requests are treated as BestEffort QoS class, which is the first to be evicted under memory pressure. Setting memory requests elevates the pod to Burstable QoS (or Guaranteed if requests equal limits), making it harder to evict. PodDisruptionBudgets protect against voluntary disruptions. Running in kube-system does not grant eviction immunity based on namespace alone.

questions.question: After applying a new NetworkPolicy, pods in namespace 'app' can no longer reach the kube-dns Service (10.96.0.10:53). What must be added to the NetworkPolicy?
options: An ingress rule allowing traffic from kube-dns to the app pods on port 53
An egress rule in the NetworkPolicy for app pods allowing UDP/TCP traffic to port 53 (to the kube-dns Service or the kube-system namespace)
A PodSelector matching kube-dns pods in the NetworkPolicy
A namespaceSelector allowing all traffic from kube-system in the ingress rules
questions.explanation: If a NetworkPolicy selects a pod and includes 'policyTypes: Egress', all egress is blocked unless explicitly allowed. DNS queries go to port 53 on the CoreDNS service. You must add an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP on port 53, either to the kube-system namespace or to the specific CoreDNS IP. Without this, DNS resolution breaks for the selected pods.

questions.question: A pod running with a projected ServiceAccount token cannot call the Kubernetes API and receives '401 Unauthorized'. The token is valid and mounted at the default path. What should you check?
options: Whether the ServiceAccount has automountServiceAccountToken: false set
Whether the ServiceAccount has a ClusterRoleBinding granting it API access
Whether the pod is running in the kube-system namespace
Whether the API server's --anonymous-auth flag is set to false
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized means the token was rejected or the identity is unknown. 401 from a ServiceAccount token is rare if the token is valid — more likely the issue is the token is for a deleted ServiceAccount, the API server's service account issuer is misconfigured, or the token has expired. However, if 403 (Forbidden) is the actual error, it means authenticated but not authorized — a missing RoleBinding. Since the question says 401, this could also indicate a token audience mismatch in newer Kubernetes versions using bound tokens.

questions.question: A node is running many pods and you want to identify which pod is consuming the most memory at this moment. Which kubectl command gives you per-pod memory usage on a specific node?
options: kubectl describe node worker-2 | grep memory
kubectl top pods --all-namespaces --sort-by=memory | grep <node-name>
kubectl top pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=spec.nodeName=worker-2 --sort-by=memory
kubectl get pods --field-selector=spec.nodeName=worker-2 -o custom-columns
questions.explanation: 'kubectl top pods' uses the metrics-server to show live CPU/memory usage. Combining --all-namespaces with --field-selector=spec.nodeName=<node> filters to pods on that node, and --sort-by=memory shows the highest consumers at the top. 'kubectl describe node' shows allocatable/allocated resources from requests, not actual live consumption. kubectl top requires metrics-server to be installed.

questions.question: A pod has been 'Terminating' for 20 minutes and will not fully delete. 'kubectl delete pod stuck-pod' was already run. What is the most likely cause and safe remediation?
options: The pod has a finalizer set in its metadata that must be removed before deletion can complete
The pod's node is offline; delete the node object to force pod removal
The pod requires --grace-period=0 to be deleted immediately
The kubelet on the pod's node needs to be restarted to flush the pod
questions.explanation: Pods stuck in Terminating are almost always held by a finalizer in metadata.finalizers. Finalizers are keys added by controllers (e.g., storage operators, admission webhooks) that must be removed before the API server will fully delete the object. The safe fix is to edit the pod and remove the finalizer entry: 'kubectl patch pod stuck-pod -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}''. Force-deleting with --grace-period=0 --force is a last resort and can leave orphaned resources.

questions.question: You need to check the container runtime version and status on a node where Docker is not installed (containerd is used). Which command should you use on the node?
options: docker info
crictl info
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep Container
ctr namespaces list
questions.explanation: 'crictl' is the CRI-compatible CLI tool for interacting with container runtimes that implement the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), such as containerd. 'crictl info' shows runtime information. 'crictl ps', 'crictl logs', and 'crictl pods' are equivalents to docker commands for CRI runtimes. 'ctr' is a low-level containerd CLI not primarily designed for Kubernetes use.

questions.question: A Deployment has a readinessProbe that fails during startup. As a result, Service traffic is never routed to the new pods. The pods are Running but not Ready. Which Deployment field can you configure so that startup failures don't count as readiness failures during a defined grace period?
options: livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds
readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds or a separate startupProbe to protect the readiness probe until the application is initialized
spec.minReadySeconds on the Deployment
spec.progressDeadlineSeconds on the Deployment
questions.explanation: readinessProbe.initialDelaySeconds delays the start of readiness checks after the container starts. Alternatively, a startupProbe (Kubernetes 1.16+) is designed specifically for slow-starting applications — it disables liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds, preventing premature failures. minReadySeconds affects when a pod is considered 'available' but doesn't protect probes. progressDeadlineSeconds is a deployment-level timeout.

questions.question: You run 'kubectl get nodes' and see node 'worker-3' in NotReady state. Running 'kubectl describe node worker-3' shows 'KubeletNotReady: container runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false reason:NetworkPluginNotReady message:Network plugin returns error'. What is the most likely fix?
options: Restart the kube-proxy daemonset pod on worker-3
Reinstall or repair the CNI plugin on the node — the CNI binary or configuration in /etc/cni/net.d/ is missing or corrupted
Reboot worker-3 to reset all network state
Delete the node object and re-join it to the cluster
questions.explanation: The 'NetworkPluginNotReady' error from the kubelet means the CNI plugin is not functioning. This typically occurs when the CNI plugin DaemonSet pod has not yet run on this node (and thus not installed the CNI binary), the CNI binary is missing from /opt/cni/bin/, or the CNI config in /etc/cni/net.d/ is absent or invalid. Ensure the CNI DaemonSet pod is running on the node and check those paths.

questions.question: A pod's application writes logs to /var/log/app.log inside the container. 'kubectl logs' shows nothing. What is the most likely reason?
options: kubectl logs only shows logs from pods that have crashed at least once
kubectl logs only captures stdout and stderr — logs written to a file inside the container are not visible via kubectl logs
The pod's ServiceAccount does not have permission to stream logs
Logs are only available after the pod has been running for at least 60 seconds
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes logging architecture captures container stdout and stderr only. If an application writes logs to a file on the container filesystem, 'kubectl logs' will show nothing. The fix is either to configure the application to log to stdout/stderr, or to use a sidecar container that tails the log file and writes to its own stdout. Alternatively, kubectl exec into the container and read the file directly.

questions.question: You need to quickly test whether a newly created ClusterRole 'deployment-viewer' provides the correct permissions. A user 'alice' should be able to 'get' and 'list' Deployments cluster-wide. Which sequence of commands validates this?
options: kubectl get clusterrole deployment-viewer -o yaml && kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep alice
kubectl auth can-i get deployments --as=alice && kubectl auth can-i list deployments --as=alice
kubectl describe clusterrolebinding alice-binding
kubectl auth reconcile --as=alice -f role.yaml
questions.explanation: 'kubectl auth can-i' with --as impersonates the user and tests a specific permission. Running it for both 'get' and 'list' on deployments validates the effective permissions without needing to inspect YAML manually. This tests the complete RBAC chain (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding). 'kubectl get clusterrole -o yaml' only shows what the role defines, not whether alice has it bound. 'kubectl auth reconcile' applies RBAC manifests, not tests permissions.
